My research centers on aging and health, especially frailty: how health declines with
age, how to measure that decline, and how gradual decline differs from acute health
shocks. I apply **econometric and biostatistical methods** to large aging panels and
health surveys (HRS, ELSA, SHARE, CHARLS, NHANES) and contribute to the Global Burden
of Disease Study. My methods include difference-in-differences with staggered adoption,
event-study and panel methods, survival analysis, multiple imputation, g-computation,
complex-survey weighting, and double/debiased machine learning.

The full list of papers and conference presentations is on the
[Publications](publications.qmd) page.

## Research interests

- Applied economics of aging and health, centered on frailty indices
- Gradual frailty in later life versus acute health shocks
- Causal inference, applied econometrics, and biostatistics for panel and survey data
- Measuring health and longevity: biomarkers, dementia case definitions, survival expectations
- Global burden of disease, health policy, and health equity
- Quantitative health sciences and clinical research methodology: cost-effectiveness and value-of-information analysis, psychometrics, survival analysis, cancer-registry cohorts
- Disaster recovery and community resilience

## Dissertation

My dissertation studies health shocks, frailty, and economic behavior in aging
populations, using panel methods and causal-inference designs.

::: {.pub-list}
::: {.pub}
**Chapter 1.** Working Through Frailty: Chronic versus Acute Health Shocks and the Margins of Labor Supply. *To be presented at the Southern Economic Association (SEA) 96th Annual Meeting, Houston, TX, November 2026.*
:::

::: {.pub}
**Chapter 2.** Falls, Missing Markets, and Labor Supply: Evidence from China.
:::

::: {.pub}
